name: Skewers
goal: You can attack a valuable piece so that, when it moves away, you win the piece behind it.

intro.text: A skewer is an attack on a valuable piece that has a less valuable piece standing behind it on the same line. When the front piece gets out of the way, you take the one behind. It works the other way round from a pin, where the piece in front is the less valuable one. Rooks, bishops and queens can all skewer, and the strongest skewers start with a check, because the king must move out of the way.

parts.title: King in front of the queen
parts.keyIdea: Check a king that has a valuable piece behind it on the same line; when the king moves, take that piece.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Black's king has just stepped to d7. Look along the seventh rank (the row numbered 7): what stands behind the king?

credit.authors: Lichess; the position is from a game played there

notes.text: 67.Qa7+: your queen moves to a7 and gives check along the seventh rank, with Black's queen on h7 directly behind the king. Black has nothing that can step in between, so the king has to leave the rank.
With the king gone from the rank, 68.Qxh7 takes Black's queen. You are left with a queen against a rook.

parts.title: King and bishop on one diagonal
parts.keyIdea: A bishop skewers along a diagonal: check the king, and win the piece that stands behind it.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Black's king has just come to e5, on the same diagonal as Black's bishop on b8. That bishop is also the piece that stops your pawn on a6 from promoting.

credit.authors: Lichess; the position is from a game played there

notes.text: 43.Bf4+: your bishop checks from f4, with Black's bishop on b8 behind the king on the same diagonal. Your king on f3 protects the bishop, so Black's king cannot take it and has to step aside.
44.Bxb8 takes the bishop. You are now a whole piece ahead, and Black no longer has a bishop to stop your a-pawn.

parts.title: Queen in front of a rook
parts.keyIdea: A skewer does not need a check: attack the queen, and when it moves, take the rook behind it.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are Black. White's queen has just moved to c3. Look at what stands behind it on the diagonal towards a1.

credit.authors: Lichess; the position is from a game played there

notes.text: 23...Bd4: your bishop attacks the queen, and White's rook on a1 stands behind it on the same diagonal. Your queen on d8 protects the bishop, so taking it would cost White the queen, and White's queen has to step away.
The queen has gone, and 24...Bxa1 takes the rook. White can take back with the other rook, but you have won a rook for a bishop.
